chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Safwan ibn Yahya, who said:

I was in the presence of Al-Reza (peace be upon him), so he sneezed. So I said to him, 'May Allah send Salawat upon you.' Then he sneezed, so I said, 'May Allah send Salawat upon you.' Then he sneezed, so I said, 'May Allah send Salawat upon you,' and I said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you! When the likes of you sneezes, should we be saying just as we are saying for each other, 'May Allah have Mercy on you', or just as we are saying?' He said: 'Yes. Are you not saying, 'May Allah send Salawat upon Muhammad and the Progeny of Muhammad'?' I said, 'Yes.' He said: 'Mercy be upon Muhammad and the Progeny of Muhammad.' I said, 'Yes, and indeed Allah has sent Salawat upon him and been Merciful to him, and rather, our Salawat upon him is a Mercy for us, and a (means) of nearness.'

key_terms.يَرْحَمُكَ اللَّهُ: May Allah have mercy on you

ai.seo_question: What is the correct response when an Imam sneezes according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the theological distinction between the general supplication for mercy ('Yarhamuk Allah') and the specific invocation of divine blessings ('Salawat') reserved for the Prophet and Imams. It highlights the Shia scholarly view that Salawat is not merely a blessing bestowed upon the recipient but serves as a means of spiritual mercy and nearness (Qurbah) for the one who recites it, thereby elevating the etiquette of responding to sneezes to a act of spiritual connection.
